prompt: How does a template read the value of a signal called `minutes`?

choices.text: `{{ minutes }}`, as with a plain field
choices.why: Without parentheses that is the signal itself, a function, and the template check refuses it.

choices.text: `{{ minutes() }}`
choices.why: Right. A signal is read by calling it, in a template as in code.

choices.text: `{{ minutes.value }}`
choices.why: That is how a resource exposes its value, as a signal you still call.

choices.text: `{{ minutes.get() }}`
choices.why: There is no `get`; the call itself reads it.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer `minutes.update((m) => m + 15)` to `minutes.set(minutes() + 15)`?

choices.text: `set` cannot take an expression
choices.why: It takes any value; the difference is where the old value comes from.

choices.text: `update` is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: Old and new in one call
choices.why: Right. The read and the write cannot drift apart.

choices.text: `set` does not notify readers
choices.why: Both notify readers of a change.

prompt: Why is a signal field in a component declared `readonly`?

choices.text: So its value cannot change
choices.why: The value changes through `set` and `update`; `readonly` is about the field.

choices.text: So nobody replaces the signal itself
choices.why: Right. The field always holds the same signal, whose value changes.

choices.text: Templates can only read `readonly` fields
choices.why: They read `protected` and `public` fields alike.

choices.text: Angular requires it for signals to work
choices.why: Signals work in a mutable field too; it would just be a trap.

prompt: In `try/computed.mts`, how many times did `  computing left` appear before `done` changed, for the two reads?

choices.text: Twice, once per read
choices.why: The second read returned the stored value.

choices.text: None, because nothing had changed
choices.why: The first read had to compute; there was no value yet.

choices.text: Once
choices.why: Right. Computed at the first read, remembered for the second.

choices.text: Three times, counting the moment it was created
choices.why: Creating it computed nothing; it is lazy.

prompt: In `try/branches.mts`, `done` changed while `showDone` was false, and `label` did not compute again. Why?

choices.text: `computed` ignores changes made with `set`
choices.why: It reacts to `set`; it reacted to `showDone.set(true)`.

choices.text: The last run never called `done()`, so it was not a dependency
choices.why: Right. A computed depends on what it read last time.

choices.text: `done` was set to a value equal to the old one
choices.why: It went from 90 to 100.

choices.text: Changes are only noticed in a component, not in a script
choices.why: The same script noticed the change to `showDone`.

prompt: A colleague reads a signal inside a `setTimeout` within a `computed`. What does the lesson warn?

choices.text: The computed throws an error at the next read
choices.why: Nothing throws; the read simply goes unnoticed.

choices.text: The timer is cancelled when the computed runs
choices.why: The timer runs; the problem is tracking.

choices.text: It turns into an effect without telling you
choices.why: It stays a computed, and a wrong one.

choices.text: That read is not tracked as a dependency
choices.why: Right. Only signals called while the function runs are tracked.

prompt: A computed computes nothing until somebody reads it: it is ___.
After `sessions().push({ minutes: 25 })`, `total()` still said 90. What would have brought the 25 in?

choices.text: `sessions.set(sessions())`, to tell the signal it changed
choices.why: The same array again; `Object.is` finds no change.

choices.text: Reading `total()` twice, so it computes again
choices.why: Nothing marked it stale, so every read returns the stored 90.

choices.text: Any update that gives the signal a new array
choices.why: Right. A new array is a change, and the copy already held the 25.

choices.text: Waiting a second for Angular to notice
choices.why: There is nothing to notice: the signal was never told.

prompt: What did `total()` print after the session of 50 minutes was added the right way?
Which of these marks a session done in a way a signal notices?

choices.text: `sessions()[0].done = true`
choices.why: That changes an object in place; the signal holds the same array.

choices.text: `sessions.update((l) => { l[0].done = true; return l; })`
choices.why: It returns the same array, so `Object.is` finds no change.

choices.text: `sessions.update((l) => l.map((s, i) => (i === 0 ? { ...s, done: true } : s)))`
choices.why: Right. A new array, with a new object for the changed session.

choices.text: `sessions.set(sessions())` after changing the object
choices.why: Setting the same array is no change.

prompt: After two clicks on `Mark 15 minutes done`, how many times had the effect run?

choices.text: Twice, once per click
choices.why: It also ran once when the component was created.

choices.text: Three times
choices.why: Right. Once at creation, once after each click.

choices.text: Once, because effects run only at creation
choices.why: It runs again whenever what it read changes.

choices.text: Four times, once per signal per click
choices.why: It runs once per round of changes, not once per signal.

prompt: A colleague writes `effect(() => this.left.set(this.planned() - this.done()))`. What does the lesson say to write instead?

choices.text: `left = computed(() => this.planned() - this.done())`
choices.why: Right. The same value, always right, with nothing to schedule.

choices.text: The same effect, inside `ngOnInit`
choices.why: Moving it does not fix copying a value into a second source of truth.

choices.text: A `@let` in the template, so the class has no field at all
choices.why: The class then cannot use the value, and the lesson's point is about deriving state.

choices.text: `left.update` in each method that changes `done`
choices.why: That spreads the derivation across every writer.

prompt: Match each job with the tool the lesson gives it.

pairs.left: a value that changes and is set by the component
a value worked out from other signals
writing to `localStorage` when a value changes
data that arrives later, with loading and error states

right_distractors: a value the template needs once

prompt: The loader asked for `/course.json` and the page said `Unexpected token '<'`. Why did `fetch` not reject?

choices.text: The dev server answered 200, as it does for every unknown address
choices.why: `--network` showed 404; addresses with an extension are not answered with the page.

choices.text: A 404 is an answer, and `fetch` only rejects when there is none
choices.why: Right. The loader has to check `response.ok`.

choices.text: `resource` swallows rejections from `fetch`
choices.why: It turns them into `error()`, which the template showed.

choices.text: The browser cached an older answer
choices.why: The request was made and answered 404 that time.

prompt: Which three signals did the template read from the resource?

choices.text: `pending()`, `failed()` and `result()`
choices.why: Those are not a resource's names.

choices.text: `isLoading()`, `error()` and `value()`
choices.why: Right. Each is a signal, read with parentheses.

choices.text: `loader()`, `params()` and `status()`
choices.why: `loader` and `params` are options you pass in, not signals you read.

choices.text: `then()`, `catch()` and `finally()`
choices.why: Those belong to a promise; a resource offers signals.

prompt: What does it mean that `resource` is marked experimental in Angular 21?

choices.text: It only works in development builds
choices.why: It works in every build; experimental is about the API's stability.

choices.text: It will be removed in Angular 22
choices.why: Nothing says so; it is the direction the framework is heading.

choices.text: Its API is not frozen between versions
choices.why: Right. The framework says so in its own documentation.

choices.text: It needs a flag in `angular.json`
choices.why: No flag is needed; the planner uses it as it is.

prompt: With `--today 2026-10-28`, how many minutes did the planner say were planned?
`isoDay` builds the date from `getFullYear`, `getMonth` and `getDate` instead of calling `toISOString()`. Why?

choices.text: `toISOString()` does not exist in Node
choices.why: It exists everywhere; the problem is its time zone.

choices.text: `toISOString()` is slower
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: `toISOString()` answers in UTC, a day ahead at 22:00 here
choices.why: Right. The planner's day is the person's day.

choices.text: `toISOString()` includes the time, which breaks the comparison
choices.why: It does, and slicing it would still give UTC's date.

prompt: `--network` listed `GET /courses.json` twice for one page. What does the lesson say comes next?

choices.text: Nothing: two requests for one file are free
choices.why: The lesson calls it wasteful now and wrong the day the copies differ.

choices.text: Caching the file in `localStorage`
choices.why: Caching would hide the duplication, not remove it.

choices.text: An input in lesson 8, then a service in lesson 11
choices.why: Right. The week hands its numbers down, then one service holds the data.

choices.text: Merging the two components into one
choices.why: The tree keeps both; the data moves instead.

prompt: Each session has a `minutes` field, and the course page will show the course's total. Which tool should compute it?

choices.text: An `effect` that sets a `total` signal
choices.why: That is the copy-into-a-signal mistake the lesson warns against.

choices.text: A method called from the template
choices.why: It works, recomputing on every check; a computed remembers.

choices.text: A `resource`, because the sessions came from a file
choices.why: The resource holds the data; the derivation is a different job.

choices.text: A `computed`
choices.why: Right. Derived from signals, remembered until they change.
